pos: n. (the Particular Baptist Society for Propagating the Gospel among the Heathen, founded at Kettering, Northamptonshire, 2 October 1792)
etymology: Baptist, from Greek baptistes; mission, from Latin mittere, to send.
biblical_def: The Baptist Missionary Society was formed in the back parlour of Widow Wallis's house at Kettering by twelve ministers who subscribed thirteen pounds, two shillings and sixpence between them. It is the beginning of the modern Protestant missionary movement in the English-speaking world. William Carey had argued the case the previous May in An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathen, and had preached the sermon whose two heads are still quoted: expect great things, attempt great things. Andrew Fuller was secretary and John Ryland and John Sutcliff among the founders; Fuller described the arrangement as Carey going down into the pit while the rest held the rope. The Society sent Carey to Bengal in 1793 and sustained Serampore for forty years. Mat 28:19 is the obligation the Enquiry argued was permanent. Rom 10:15 is the rope-holders' clause, that preachers must be sent.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending; persons sent to propagate religion; and heathen, as pagans; people who worship idols, or are unacquainted with the true God.
webster_full: MIS'SION, n. A sending or being sent, usually the latter; persons sent; any number of persons appointed by authority to perform any service.
MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion.
HE'ATHEN, n. A pagan; a Gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
corruption_summary: Thirteen pounds and twelve ministers in a back parlour began the modern missionary movement.
corruption_paragraphs: Carey's Enquiry had to argue a point that now seems obvious: that the Great Commission was not discharged by the apostles and expired with them. The hyper-Calvinism of the English Particular Baptists had taught that God would convert the heathen in His own time without human means, and the argument wore the dress of reverence. Mat 28:19 and Mat 28:20 answer it, since the promise of Christ's presence runs to the end of the world and a promise outlasting the apostles belongs to a command that outlasts them too.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The present-day equivalent of the hyper-Calvinist objection is softer: that evangelizing other cultures is presumptuous. Psa 2:8 gives the Son the heathen for His inheritance and the uttermost parts of the earth for His possession, which settles whose presumption is in question. The principle to recover is the rope-holders' clause of Rom 10:15, that sending is a church's duty and not a specialist agency's hobby.

“Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance” (Psa 2:8) — whose earth it is.

pos: n. (the Missionary Society, founded in London 1795, afterwards the London Missionary Society; interdenominational, in practice chiefly Congregational)
biblical_def: The London Missionary Society was founded in September 1795 at a meeting in the Castle and Falcon by ministers and laymen of several denominations — Congregational, Presbyterian, Anglican, Methodist — on the declared principle that it would not send any form of church government to the heathen but the gospel, leaving converts to order themselves from Scripture. Its first venture was the ship Duff, which carried thirty missionaries to Tahiti in 1796, a mission that produced nothing for fifteen years and then saw the island turn. It sent Robert Morrison to China, John Williams to the Pacific, Robert Moffat and David Livingstone to Africa, and James Gilmour to Mongolia. Its founding principle proved generous and unworkable in detail, since Scripture does teach a polity; but the instinct, that an English denomination is not the gospel, was sound. Mar 16:15 is the commission. Act 1:8 the geography. Rev 7:9 the end in view, a multitude of all nations before the throne.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a society as a number of persons united for some particular purpose; and interdenominational usage follows from denomination, a class or society called by the same name.
webster_full: SOCI'ETY, n. A number of persons united, either for government or for mutual benefit; an association for religious or charitable purposes.
DENOMINA'TION, n. The act of naming; a name or appellation; a class or society of individuals called by the same name.
MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.
corruption_summary: It declared it would export the gospel and no church order, which was impossible and better than the alternative.
corruption_paragraphs: The fundamental principle of 1795 cannot be carried out strictly. A missionary must baptize somebody somehow and must either appoint elders or not, and the New Testament is not silent on these matters. What the founders were refusing was the export of English denominational machinery, establishment, patronage, parish systems, as though these were apostolic. Mat 28:20 commands the teaching of all things whatsoever Christ commanded, which includes His commands about the church, and excludes everything He did not command.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern failure runs the other way. Agencies now sometimes export a managerial model, a brand and a funding apparatus while treating doctrine as the adaptable part, which inverts the 1795 instinct exactly. Rev 7:9 shows the end God intends, a great multitude of all nations and kindreds and people and tongues before the throne, which is neither uniformity nor indifference.

Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, a language; Revelation 7:9.

“unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8) — Tahiti, China, Mongolia.
“of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) — the end in view.

pos: n. (the Society for Missions to Africa and the East, founded 1799 by members of the Eclectic Society; afterwards the Church Missionary Society)
etymology: Church, from Greek kuriakon, belonging to the Lord; mission, from Latin mittere, to send.
biblical_def: The Church Missionary Society grew out of the Eclectic Society's discussion of 18 March 1799 on the best method of propagating the gospel among the heathen, and was constituted a month later by sixteen clergy and nine laymen, with John Venn in the chair. Its early principles were that it should follow God's leading rather than a plan, begin small, and look for men wherever they could be found; since no English clergyman would go, its first missionaries were German Lutherans trained at Berlin. Josiah Pratt as secretary built it into a worldwide body. Henry Martyn went to India under the chaplaincy rather than the Society, but out of the same circle. The CMS worked in Sierra Leone, India, New Zealand and East Africa, and was from the beginning committed to raising native ministry rather than permanent European oversight. Act 16:9 is the Macedonian pattern it looked for. Mat 9:38 the prayer that opened the question.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines providence as the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; and mission, as a sending or being sent.
webster_full: PROV'IDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures. A manifestation of the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
MIS'SION, n. A sending or being sent; persons sent; any number of persons appointed by authority to perform any service.
AGEN'CY, n. The quality of acting; the state of being in action; action; operation; instrumentality.
scriptures: Act 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Isa 6:8
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
corruption_summary: No Englishman would go, so they sent Germans, and the Society's rule was to follow the open door rather than a plan.
corruption_paragraphs: The CMS principle of following Providence is often misremembered as passivity. It was not. The Society made plans, raised money and trained men; what it refused was to decide in advance which fields God must open. Act 16:9 is the biblical shape of that, a vision of a man of Macedonia saying come over and help us, which redirected an apostolic journey that already had a plan.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isa 6:8's order: the Lord asks whom shall I send and who will go for us, and the answer is a volunteer, not a draft. The Society's willingness to take German Lutherans when English clergy would not volunteer is a reproach that still reads well. Mat 9:38 commands the prayer, and a church that prays it should expect to be answered out of its own number.

“Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest” (Mat 9:38) — the Eclectic question of 1799.
“Here am I; send me” (Isa 6:8) — and at first no Englishman said it.

pos: n. (the Scottish Missionary Society, founded at Edinburgh 1796, with a parallel body at Glasgow)
etymology: Scottish, from Old English Scottas; society, from Latin societas, fellowship.
biblical_def: The Scottish Missionary Society was founded at Edinburgh in February 1796, with a companion Glasgow society formed the same month, in the wave of societies that followed Carey's sailing. Its founding was fiercely opposed in the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland that May, where a motion of support was defeated on the argument that the heathen must first be civilized and that sending men abroad while Scotland had vacant parishes was imprudent. The societies proceeded without the Assembly. They sent missionaries to Sierra Leone, to Russia's Tatar frontier at Karass, to Jamaica and to India, and they funded Robert Moffat's training. Within forty years the Assembly had reversed itself and Alexander Duff went out as the Church of Scotland's own missionary. Mat 9:37 and Mat 9:38 are the texts the opponents turned on their head. Act 1:8 does not make Jerusalem a precondition for the uttermost part; it makes them simultaneous.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prudence as wisdom applied to practice; and civilization, as the state of being refined in manners from the grossness of savage life.
webster_full: PRU'DENCE, n. Wisdom applied to practice; that sagacity or shrewdness which enables a person to judge of what is best, in view of all circumstances.
CIVILIZA'TION, n. The act of civilizing, or the state of being civilized; the state of being refined in manners.
ASSEM'BLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place; in Scotland, the highest court of the church.
scriptures: Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
corruption_summary: The General Assembly voted that the heathen must be civilized first, and the societies went anyway.
corruption_paragraphs: The civilize-first argument of 1796 deserves to be named as the error it was. It assumes the gospel is suited only to minds already improved, which reverses the order of Act 1:8 and contradicts the whole book of Acts, where the gospel went to pagan sailors, jailers and slaves before it improved anybody. The missionary experience of the next century settled the question empirically as well: literacy, medicine and the ending of cruelties followed the gospel rather than preceding it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern inversion is worth noting, that mission should be development work with the preaching left out, which is the 1796 argument with the sequence made permanent. Mat 9:37 says the harvest is plenteous; a church that will not send until conditions improve has decided the harvest can wait. Mar 16:15 names the audience as every creature, in whatever state he is found.

usage: “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — against the prudent.
“both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea” (Act 1:8) — and the uttermost part, at the same time.
“preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — in whatever state he is found.

pos: n. (Serampore, a Danish settlement on the Hooghly above Calcutta; the mission station of Carey, Marshman and Ward from 1800)
etymology: Bengali Shrirampur, the town of Sri Rama; Danish Frederiksnagore.
biblical_def: Serampore was a small Danish colony fifteen miles above Calcutta, and the three Baptist missionaries settled there in 1800 because the East India Company would not permit missionary work in its own territory. William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward formed what became known as the Serampore Trio and lived under a common agreement: pooled income, shared household, a monthly reading of their covenant, and a mission run as a family. In thirty-four years they translated the Scriptures in whole or part into about forty languages and dialects, set up a printing press and a paper mill, founded Serampore College in 1818 to train Indian ministers in their own tongues, campaigned against sati and infanticide, and published the first Bengali newspaper. Isa 55:11 is the promise under the press. Psa 68:11 describes what came off it. Mat 28:19 is the commission the Company tried to exclude.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a press as a machine for printing; and translation, as the act of turning into another language; version.
webster_full: PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed; a machine for printing; called a printing press.
TRANSLA'TION, n. The act of turning into another language; interpretation; a version.
COL'LEGE, n. A society of persons engaged in common pursuits; an edifice appropriated to the use of students.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
corruption_summary: Three men under one roof translated Scripture into forty tongues on a press they built themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: The Serampore agreement is the part most worth imitating and least imitated. The three read it aloud together three times a year, and it bound them to set no value on money except as it advanced the kingdom, to live simply, to esteem one another, and to keep the Indian people constantly in view as the mission's object rather than its background. Ecc 4 and 1Co 3:6 both bear on it: distinct labours, one increase from God, and no competition between the labourers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It does rebuke two things. First, the separation of translation from church planting, as though the text could be delivered and the congregation left to someone else; Serampore did both. Second, the assumption that commercial interests and missions are natural allies. The East India Company excluded missionaries for decades because conversion was bad for trade, and Isa 55:11 is the answer to that calculation, since the word accomplishes what God pleases regardless of what a company prefers.

pos: n. (Joshua Marshman, 1768–1837, missionary at Serampore, schoolmaster, Chinese and Sanskrit scholar)
etymology: Hebrew Yehoshua, the LORD is salvation; Marshman, a dweller by a marsh.
biblical_def: Joshua Marshman was a weaver's son from Wiltshire who worked as a bookseller's assistant and read everything he handled, became master of a Baptist school at Bristol, and sailed for Bengal in 1799. At Serampore he and his wife Hannah ran the boarding schools whose fees paid for much of the mission — the Trio funded themselves and returned their earnings to the common purse. He learned Sanskrit, Bengali and Chinese, translated the Bible into Chinese and published it in 1822, produced the first English translation of Confucius's Analects, and wrote a Chinese grammar. He also led the mission's long campaign against sati, the burning of widows, supplying the statistics that eventually moved the government to abolish it in 1829. Jas 1:27 and the care of widows is not an incidental connection. 2Ti 2:2 is the schoolmaster's text. Isa 55:11 the translator's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; and suttee usage follows from immolation, the act of sacrificing.
webster_full: GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
IMMOLA'TION, n. The act of sacrificing; a sacrifice offered.
SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university.
scriptures: Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
corruption_summary: He paid for the mission by running schools and spent twenty years counting burned widows until the law changed.
corruption_paragraphs: Marshman's campaign against sati is a case study in how Christian social reform actually proceeds. He did not begin with denunciation; he began with counting, sending observers to the burning grounds around Calcutta to record names, dates and ages, and published the figures year after year until they could not be dismissed as missionary exaggeration. Jas 1:27 names visiting widows in their affliction as pure religion, and a widow about to be burned is the limiting case.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern objection, that opposing sati was cultural imperialism, is worth answering plainly: the practice killed women, Indian reformers such as Ram Mohan Roy opposed it alongside the missionaries, and a religion that cannot say a burning is wrong has nothing to say at all. Isa 55:11 and the translation work went forward in the same hands at the same time; the gospel and the rescue were never two projects.

pos: n. (William Ward, 1769–1823, printer of the Serampore mission, author of a four-volume account of Hindu religion)
etymology: Old English weard, a watchman or guardian; William, Germanic, resolute protector.
biblical_def: William Ward was a printer and newspaper editor at Derby and Hull, a political radical in his youth, baptized in 1796 and sent to Bengal in 1799. Carey had met him years before and told him that if he ever got to India he would need a printer for the Scriptures; Ward remembered it. At Serampore he set up and ran the press that produced Scripture in some forty tongues, cast types for Bengali, Devanagari, Chinese and other scripts, and rebuilt the whole works after a fire destroyed it in 1812 — the type punches survived and the press was running again within months. His Account of the Writings, Religion and Manners of the Hindoos was for decades the standard English description. He also toured Britain and America raising money for Serampore College. Isa 55:11 is the promise his press served. Col 4:3 is the prayer he lived on, that God would open a door of utterance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a printer as one that prints books, pamphlets or papers; and a type, as a printing letter; the letters or characters used in printing.
webster_full: PRINT'ER, n. One that prints books, pamphlets or papers.
TYPE, n. A printing letter; the letters or characters used by printers, cast in metal.
FOUND'ERY, n. The art of casting metals into various forms; a house and works for casting metals.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Col 4:3
Withal praying also for us, that God would open unto us a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds:
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
corruption_summary: The press burned to the ground in 1812 with the type punches intact, and was printing again before the year was out.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1812 fire destroyed manuscripts, paper, and the work of years, and Carey's account of it is one of the great Christian responses to loss: he observed that the Lord had laid him low that he might look more simply to Him. Ward recast and reprinted. 1Co 15:58 is the word for that recovery, stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding, and the labour is not in vain in the Lord even when the warehouse is ash.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that technical trades are ministry callings. Ward was a tradesman whose skill no amount of theological learning could have replaced, and the Serampore translations exist because a Hull printer took his press to Bengal. Col 4:3 asks for an open door of utterance, and in 1800 that door was a printing press.

pos: n. (Claudius Buchanan, 1766–1815, chaplain of the East India Company, advocate of an Indian church establishment and of Scripture translation)
etymology: Latin Claudius, a Roman gens name; Buchanan, from a Stirlingshire place-name.
biblical_def: Claudius Buchanan ran away from Scotland to London as a young man, lived loosely, was converted under John Newton's ministry, and was sent by Henry Thornton to Cambridge and then to Bengal as a Company chaplain in 1797. As vice-provost of the College of Fort William he promoted the translation of Scripture into the languages of India and funded much of Carey's work from the Company's own establishment. Travelling through the south in 1806 he visited the Syrian Christians of Malabar, an ancient church which had kept the Scriptures in Syriac for centuries, obtained a copy of their Syriac Bible, and published Christian Researches in Asia in 1811. That book, and his preaching tour of England, did more than anything else to force the 1813 renewal of the Company's charter to admit missionaries. Act 16:9 is the shape of his findings. Rev 7:9 is what Malabar showed him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chaplain as a clergyman who performs divine service in the army or navy, or in a family; and research, as diligent inquiry or examination.
webster_full: CHAP'LAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has a chapel, or who performs service in a chapel. A clergyman who belongs to a ship of war, or to a regiment of soldiers.
RESEARCH', n. Diligent inquiry or examination in seeking facts or principles; laborious or continued search after truth.
CHAR'TER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
scriptures: Act 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Psa 96:3
Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.
corruption_summary: He found an ancient church in Malabar that had kept the Scriptures in Syriac while Europe assumed India was unevangelized.
corruption_paragraphs: Buchanan's discovery corrects a persistent English assumption that the gospel travels outward from Europe. The Malabar Christians traced their church to the apostolic age and had maintained a Syriac Scripture and a liturgy through centuries without Western help. Rev 7:9 anticipates exactly this, a multitude of all nations and kindreds and tongues, and a missionary movement that forgets it will treat every field as empty ground.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two cautions belong here. The Syrian church had real doctrinal defects which Buchanan did not pretend away, and the proper response to an ancient national church is neither to absorb it nor to ignore it, but to put the Scriptures into its people's hands — which is what he did, printing the Syriac Bible. Isa 55:11 is the reason that is always the right move. Psa 96:3 is the duty that remains whatever is found on the ground.

“of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) — already there before him.
“Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3) — the standing duty.

pos: n. (Henry Nott, 1774–1844, bricklayer, missionary of the Duff to Tahiti, translator of the Tahitian Bible)
etymology: English Nott, from Old English hnott, close-cropped; Henry, Germanic, ruler of the home.
biblical_def: Henry Nott was a Bromsgrove bricklayer with little schooling who sailed on the Duff in 1796 as one of the London Missionary Society's first thirty missionaries to Tahiti. Within a few years almost all the others had died, fled or abandoned the work; Nott stayed, through war, plague and the mission's collapse, for the better part of fifty years. For fifteen years there was not one convert. He learned Tahitian thoroughly, became the translator of the whole Bible into it, completed in 1838, and lived to see the island and much of eastern Polynesia profess Christianity after the king's conversion in 1812 broke the old order. He is the plainest refutation available of the idea that missions require educated men. Psa 126:6 is his biography: he that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing. 1Co 15:58 is the promise he held for fifteen barren years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perseverance as persistence in any business or enterprise undertaken; and barren, as not producing fruit; unfruitful.
webster_full: PERSEVE'RANCE, n. Persistence in any business or enterprise undertaken; continued pursuit or prosecution of any design.
BAR'REN, a. Not producing young, or offspring; not producing fruit; unfruitful; sterile.
VER'SION, n. A translation; the rendering of thoughts from one language into another.
scriptures: He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
corruption_summary: Fifteen years in Tahiti without one convert, and then the whole island, and then a Bible in their language.
corruption_paragraphs: Nott is the standing argument against measuring a mission by its early returns. For fifteen years the Tahitian mission would have failed any modern assessment: no converts, dead and deserting colleagues, a station abandoned at one point to the Australian colony. 1Co 3:6 explains why the metric is wrong, since planting and watering are the labourers' work and the increase is God's, on a timetable He does not publish.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest caution is that the Tahitian turning came through the conversion of a king and carried with it the mixed results such turnings always have, nominal profession among them. That does not cancel the work; it describes it. Psa 126:6 promises the sower will come again with rejoicing and does not promise the harvest will be unmixed. Isa 55:11 guarantees the word, not the convenience of its timing.

usage: “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed” (Psa 126:6) — fifteen years of it.
“your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) — held with no evidence.
“but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) — on His own timetable.

pos: n. (James Chalmers, 1841–1901, London Missionary Society missionary to Rarotonga and New Guinea, killed at Goaribari)
etymology: Scottish Chalmers, from Old French chambre, a chamberlain; James, from Hebrew Ya'aqob.
biblical_def: James Chalmers was an Argyllshire boy who volunteered for the mission field at fifteen after hearing a letter from Fiji read in Sunday school. He served ten years in Rarotonga and then from 1877 in New Guinea, where he spent twenty-four years exploring and preaching along a coast and up rivers no European had entered, travelling almost always unarmed and generally alone. Robert Louis Stevenson, who knew him, called him a man of the same stamp as the greatest. In April 1901 he and his young colleague Oliver Tomkins landed at Goaribari Island, were received into a long house, and were killed and eaten the same morning; the punitive expedition that followed was not what he would have wanted. Rev 2:10 is the promise over his death. Act 20:24 is the sentence he lived by, counting not his life dear unto himself so that he might finish his course with joy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pioneer as one whose business is to prepare the way; and martyr, as one who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith.
webster_full: PIONEE'R, n. One whose business is to march before an army, to repair the road or clear it of obstructions; one who goes before to prepare the way.
M'ARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith, or by reason of his adherence to it.
CAN'NIBAL, n. A human being that eats human flesh; a man-eater or anthropophagite.
scriptures: But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
corruption_summary: Twenty-four years alone and unarmed along the New Guinea coast, and then a long house at Goaribari.
corruption_paragraphs: Chalmers went unarmed on principle, holding that a missionary who carries a gun has announced what he expects of the people he has come to. The policy cost him his life and he knew the risk precisely; he had written about it. Act 20:24 is his own standard, that none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself. The sentence is not bravado; it is a man's calculation of what the ministry he received is worth.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two things are often said about such deaths and both are wrong. The first treats them as waste, which Rev 2:10 answers with the crown of life promised to the faithful unto death. The second treats them as a licence for reprisal, and the British punitive raid after Goaribari killed people who had nothing to do with it. Rev 12:11 names the weapons, the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, and lists no others.
roots_summary: Greek dromos (G1408), a course; stephanos (G4735), a crown; marturia (G3141), testimony.
roots_lines: Greek dromos (G1408) — a course, a race; Acts 20:24.
usage: “neither count I my life dear unto myself” (Act 20:24) — twenty-four years unarmed.
“be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10) — Goaribari, 1901.
“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — and named no other weapon.
